strengths: The distinction between sparsity of the whitened mean difference and sparsity of the discriminant direction is useful. The analysis has an identifiable audience studying classification under strong latent factors and diverging covariance spikes.

Entrywise eigenspace perturbation bounds are a well-motivated tool for analyzing whitening and coordinate screening. The main algorithm and its relationship to CAT-LDA and sparse discriminant methods are explained clearly.

The experiments include 200 Monte Carlo replications, several covariance structures, two gene-expression datasets, and supplementary sensitivity analysis. Reporting both classification error and representation dimension provides useful empirical information.
weaknesses: Necessary correction: The QDA reduction in Eq. (5.5), and consequently Theorem 6, is invalid under the stated assumptions. Sparsity of the whitened means does not eliminate covariance information outside their support. For a concrete counterexample, let B = I + p uuᵀ with u = 1/√p, set Σ₁ = B, Σ₂ = 4B, μ₁ = B^(1/2)e₁, and μ₂ = 2μ₁. These satisfy the relevant spike, coherence, and mean-sparsity conditions, with both whitened means equal to e₁. The reduced population score uses only Y₁ = [B^(-1/2)Z]₁, distributed as N(1,1) or N(2,4). Even its optimal threshold has approximately 30.5% error under equal priors, whereas variance information in the remaining coordinates makes the full Bayes error tend to zero. Repairing this requires changing the reduction or substantially restricting the theorem. This is a substantive failure of the evidence criterion for an advertised contribution.

Necessary correction: The main LDA theorem exceeds its supplied proof. Theorem 3 asserts almost-sure Bayes consistency under log p = o(n), but Section 8.4 concludes only convergence in probability of the discriminant score and explicitly requires log n · log p = o(n). The transition to almost-sure conditional-risk convergence is not established. Furthermore, the proofs assume fixed sparsity; Remark 1 explicitly leaves growing sparsity untreated, so the abstract's sparsity-dependent condition should not suggest that this broader regime has been proved. Supply the missing arguments or narrow the statements and corresponding extensions.

Necessary correction: Section 7.3 incorrectly asserts Bayes optimality of Fisher LDA for general elliptical distributions with unrestricted class priors. For a shared radial density h, the Bayes comparison involves log h(r₁²) − log h(r₂²) plus the log prior odds. This generally produces a different boundary from Gaussian LDA when priors are unequal; sub-Gaussian tails do not resolve this issue. Restrict the claim to appropriate cases, such as equal priors with a common decreasing radial density, or analyze the appropriate classifier.

Necessary correction: The numerical reporting needs verification. Several entries for ρ = 0.8 exactly repeat those for ρ = 0.7 in Tables 1 and 2. Under the stated Model 1, the theoretical Bayes error at ρ = 0.8 is approximately 0.022%, whereas Table 1 reports an oracle error of 0.19%; with 40,000 test predictions across replications, ordinary Monte Carlo variation is not a convincing explanation. The accompanying claim of highest accuracy also contradicts the lower errors reported for competing methods at ρ = 0.8 and 0.9. Correct the tables and align the interpretation with the verified results.

Optional improvements: End-to-end timing, including preprocessing and tuning, would substantiate the computational comparison. Broader sensitivity experiments would also clarify the practical reliability of the 90% explained-variance rule; testing one additional retained component in one setting provides limited support for general claims that overestimating the rank is harmless.
